newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Supply best answer to land speculation - HK's Tsang.
newsitem.headline: Supply best answer to land speculation - HK's Tsang.

text.p: The best way to balance Hong Kong's property market against pressure from rampant speculation was to boost supply to the maximum extent possible, Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said on Thursday.

Tsang said he was concerned by evidence that speculation at the high end of property market was going on at a rampant pace, as excessive speculation induced spreading of upward price pressures across the entire market.

"A short term price spiral could lead genuine home buyers in the mass market into haphazard purchase decisions which strain their affordability," Tsang said in a speech to the Chinese Manufacturers Association.

"Should the situation develop into a speculative bubble, the risk of precipitating an abrupt downturn would be very much greater, with adverse implications not only for the property sector but also for the banks and the economy at large.
"Too much heat in the market is not a healthy development," he said.
But Tsang said that curbing demand artificially was not the best way to fight the problem.

"Given enthusiastic response to sales of flats, developers should all be keen to get more projects going. If we can make more land available for development, the volume of housing supply in the pipeline would grow and prices would stabilise.

"We must work harder on larger supply across the whole spectrum of land sale, conversion of land use in form of residential development and streamlining of planning or approval procedures," Tsang noted.

A recent spiralling of top-end flat prices have caused an outcry in Hong Kong and the government recently set up an inter-departmental committee to look into the issue, raising concerns about possible intervention in the market.
In an industry initiative to tackle the issue, developer Sun Hung Kai Properties Ltd set up a new system for handling an upcoming flat sale aimed at curbing speculators.

The company will limit the number of buyers registering as limited companies, which speculators are said to use to pay less tax and avoid resale restrictions, to a maximum of 20 out of every 100 registered buyers.
